slides.title: From chiplet opportunity to system architecture
slides.transcript: Welcome to F C S A: Architecting Interoperable Chiplet Systems. This course turns chiplet integration into a set of architectural decisions you can explain and review. You should already be comfortable with chiplet partitioning, packaging, and die-to-die communication. The Open Chiplet Economy learning plan provides that foundation. Here, we will use Foundation Chiplet System Architecture, version one point one point zero, to connect a system boundary to chiplet roles, interface obligations, coordinated boot, and composed trust. The goal is an informed integration review. Completing the course does not certify a hardware implementation.
slides.subtitle: Define the boundary, then interpret the claim.

slides.title: The decisions you will learn to make
slides.transcript: Our running case adds an accelerator to a Compute and Hub system. First, establish what belongs to the system and how to read a requirement. Then classify the chiplets, trace their connections, examine trust, and request the evidence needed for integration. Use the linked workbook as part of the course: pause for its five exercises and compare your reasoning with the worked responses. Narration, diagram review, ten questions, and the workbook together are intended to take about seventy-five to ninety minutes. The two linked Summit recordings offer optional deeper viewing outside that estimate.
slides.subtitle: Use the running integration case and workbook to turn the architecture into decisions.

slides.title: Reuse needs shared expectations
slides.transcript: Start with a system design whose processing, memory, and control functions were planned together. Partition that design across chiplets, and some relationships that were internal now cross independently designed boundaries. A working physical link does not settle what each chiplet provides, what its neighbor expects, or how the complete system behaves. F C S A makes those expectations explicit through system types, chiplet types, and interface requirements. Protocol and transport mappings add implementation detail where suitable standards exist; some mappings remain to be defined. Now reuse the same compute chiplet in another configuration. Its identity stays the same, but the surrounding system changes. The integrator must check the applicable roles and interfaces again. Design and profile requirements add the detail needed for the intended product. Reuse therefore begins with a shared architectural contract; it does not end with a connection.

figure.alt: Partitioning exposes architectural obligations across a die boundary; packaging alone does not define the system.
figure.caption: Partitioning exposes cross-chiplet obligations. Reuse needs explicit roles, interfaces, and product requirements.
figure.master_timeline: One narration-synchronized pass, 1551 frames at 30fps; final two seconds held.

slides.title: Foundation, design, and profile
slides.transcript:
Read the architecture as three extending layers. The foundation establishes common concepts and basic requirements without choosing every detail of a product. A design specification adds requirements for a particular system design. For example, that layer could specialize the architecture for an instruction set. A profile then extends a design specification for a market, deployment environment, or focused function. The higher layer includes the lower layer's requirements and adds to them. This is a requirements relationship, not a menu in which a profile replaces the foundation.

F C S A concentrates on a system that could have been a monolithic design and is now partitioned across chiplets. An operating system or hypervisor provides a useful boundary for the single system software image. Some packaged devices remain abstracted by established peripheral or memory standards. F C S A can describe the system that uses those devices without defining every device inside the package.

There is another useful boundary: a chiplet type can apply to a composite structure integrated as one unit. The tightly coupled internal dies of that structure are not automatically independent F C S A chiplet types. Before drawing a type box around every die, establish the unit that the architecture actually exposes. These distinctions keep our accelerator example focused on the obligations that matter.

figure.alt: Design requirements extend the foundation; profile requirements extend a design. A physical die is not automatically an independent FCSA integration unit.
figure.caption: Each layer adds requirements to the layers below. A type may describe a composite integration unit.

entries.text: Higher layers include the lower-layer requirements

slides.title: Read a rule before making a claim
slides.transcript:
F C S A uses content classes to separate requirements from explanation. Declarations define concepts, terms, structures, or encodings. Rules describe required behavior. Both are normative. Goals, information, rationale, implementation notes, and software guidance help interpretation, but are informative. A useful reading method is to identify the statement class, read the surrounding section, and then check applicability. An isolated rule identifier is not enough context for an integration decision.

Compliance levels add another dimension. Level zero includes the basic functional and interface rules for the stated chiplet or system type. Level one adds requirements and includes the applicable level-zero rules. Full compliance includes the applicable remaining requirements, including rules without a displayed level. A higher level does not make lower-level obligations disappear. Applicability still depends on the implementation and the feature being considered.

In a supplier discussion, replace an unqualified compatibility claim with a precise statement of the specification version, system or chiplet type, level, interfaces, and evidence. Also identify the design and profile requirements needed by this product. A declaration of compliance is a claim to investigate against those obligations; the course itself provides no certification process. Keep the version and level attached to the scope so that different teams can evaluate the same claim.
rows: Normative concepts and behavior; read in context
Applicable basic functional and interface rules
Applicable Level 0 rules plus Level 1 rules
All applicable requirements, including unmarked rules

slides.title: Navigate from your role to the relevant rules
slides.transcript:
A system designer starts with system requirements and chooses the system type, chiplet roles, quantities, and combinations. A standalone chiplet designer starts with intended deployments and the required functionality and interfaces. These are two entry points into the same specification. Neither role can stop after reading only a marketing description of a type.

For our running case, the integrator records a Compute and Hub system, an accelerator under consideration, and the software boundary. The next questions concern coherent caches, address translation, and the interfaces required by the chosen pair. After selecting the roles, the review moves to functional interface requirements, common boot and control components, implementation mappings, and security. The route through the chapters follows dependencies rather than document length.

Open workbook exercise one. In the first scenario, application processors share one operating system while a separate accelerator contributes to that system. In the second, two independently managed systems share a package. Write the boundary of the proposed F C S A claim for each. Then draft the minimum information missing from the sentence, this package is F C S A compatible. Spend about six minutes before reading the worked response. The aim is to make the claim testable, while leaving detailed type selection for the next module.

slides.title: A clear scope makes a useful claim
slides.transcript: The system boundary is the starting point for a useful F C S A review. Foundation, design, and profile requirements build on one another. Normative declarations and rules need their surrounding context, and a compliance level must be tied to an applicable type and version. You have used those ideas to turn a broad compatibility statement into a reviewable claim. Keep the scope statement from exercise one: it will determine which chiplet roles and interfaces belong in the topology we examine next.

slides.title: Compute & Hub or Compute Tile?
slides.transcript: Compare the responsibilities, not just the arrangement of rectangles. A Compute and Hub system requires at least one Compute One chiplet and at least one Hub chiplet. Compute One supplies application processing. The Hub provides access to system memory and input-output resources. A primary Hub coordinates system management and security when there are several Hubs. In a Compute Tile system, at least one Compute Two chiplet combines application processing with direct access to memory and input-output resources. With several Compute Two chiplets, one is primary and coordinates those system functions. The contrast is not an absolute ban on other capabilities: Compute One can also contain or directly connect to system memory, and implementations can satisfy multiple types. Start with the required roles, then inspect each chiplet's capabilities and required interfaces. A familiar-looking topology alone does not establish the classification.

figure.alt: Compute & Hub separates application processing from Hub functions; Compute Tile uses Compute 2 chiplets with combined responsibilities.
figure.caption: Compare required roles: Compute 1 plus Hub, or Compute 2. Then verify functions and interfaces.

slides.title: Match a role to a chiplet type
slides.transcript:
There are ten defined chiplet types. Three establish the main compute and hub roles: Compute one, Compute two, and Hub. Five expansion types distinguish fully coherent processing from input output coherent processing and then distinguish translation arrangements. The remaining two types provide input output functions: the input output Chiplet and the input output Controller Chiplet. This grouping is a navigation aid; the exact functionality and interface rules remain in each type's section.

A type is more than a product category. It specifies on-chiplet functionality and a mandatory interface set. A vendor may implement additional functions and interfaces. A chiplet can satisfy more than one type when it meets the requirements of each, although integration-specific configuration may be needed. The type decision is therefore not always an exclusive choice among ten labels.

For example, knowing that a component accelerates inference does not establish whether it has coherent caches or where addresses are translated. Nor does a process node, package footprint, or supplier name answer those questions. Those facts matter elsewhere in engineering, but they cannot replace the architectural evidence. Use the type map to find the likely section, then test the candidate against its required capabilities and interfaces. The workbook contains the full names so that the shortened labels on a topology do not become an ambiguous supplier declaration.
rows: Fully Coherent Expansion; Fully Coherent Expansion (Remote Translation)

slides.title: Coherence and translation change the interface
slides.transcript:
Separate two questions. First, does the device contain coherent caches? A fully coherent processing device does, and makes coherent accesses to the rest of the system. An input output coherent processing device has no coherent cache of its own, although its accesses to the rest of the system are coherent. Do not use the word coherent without stating which behavior is meant.

Second, where are memory addresses translated and access permissions checked? The translated, untranslated, and remote-translation types make different arrangements visible at the boundary. Follow an access from the processing device toward system-addressable memory and locate the memory management function. Record the address representation on each side of that boundary and the component responsible for protection. The specification's type diagrams and interface requirements make those responsibilities concrete.

These questions interact, but they are not interchangeable. A coherent cache does not tell you where translation occurs. A translated address does not establish that the device holds coherent cache lines. For our accelerator, ask for both facts, then ask which interface requirements the implementation satisfies. Until those answers are known, the classification remains a candidate. Treat this diagram as a way to structure the review, rather than as a complete address-translation design for a product.

figure.alt: Coherent caching and address translation are separate classification axes. Trace both before assigning a type.
figure.caption: Coherent caching and translation are separate facts. Locate both before assigning a chiplet type.

slides.title: Classify the next integration
slides.transcript:
The candidate accelerator joins a Compute and Hub system. The first supplier description says it performs coherent accesses, but that phrase leaves a critical ambiguity. Ask whether it contains caches that participate in coherency with other chiplets, or instead relies on input output coherency without its own coherent cache. Then locate translation and access protection, and request the relevant functional interfaces and configuration restrictions.

The host responsibilities matter as much as the accelerator's feature list. An untranslated or remote-translation arrangement needs the matching system-side functions and the correct interface behavior. A candidate that advertises a capability in one configuration may require different settings when used as another F C S A type. Include the intended system composition and deployment when asking for evidence.

Spend about seven minutes on workbook exercise two. It provides two supplier responses with different cache and translation behavior. Propose the next specification sections to read and list the evidence still missing. You do not need to invent a complete chiplet from the response. A useful outcome is a defensible candidate classification plus a small set of questions that would confirm or reject it. This habit avoids turning an incomplete data sheet into a confident integration commitment.

slides.title: A die-to-die link carries several contracts
slides.transcript:
Use the Hub-to-Compute connection as a concrete reading exercise. Chapter five identifies the functional relationships: coherent memory traffic, interrupts, security communication, system control, boot code image loading, boot sequence control, and debug. These are architectural obligations for the pair. They are not seven interchangeable names for one high-speed link.

Chapter seven then maps interface requirements to protocols and transports. The protocol defines the exchanged meaning and behavior. The transport supplies the mechanism carrying it. Read both dimensions and check versions for equality or mutual compatibility. F C S A references available standards rather than defining every new mechanism itself. Some mapping entries are explicitly marked to be defined. Preserve those gaps in the integration review instead of filling them with an assumption.

For example, the published level-one coherent-memory protocol rule names Amba C H I Chip-to-Chip. The Summit discussion also considers future alignment with Amba C two C. A future direction does not silently replace the mapping in version one point one point zero. Likewise, a transport entry cannot prove that an unspecified protocol has been settled. Build a pairwise record with function, applicable rule and level, protocol, transport, version, and unresolved agreement. That record is much more informative than writing one interface-standard name beside a line.

slides.title: An interface must exist when it is needed
slides.transcript:
F C S A describes chiplet activity states because an interface can be physically present and still be unavailable. Inactive, secure boot, initial boot, operational, and power saving describe different availability conditions. Inactive chiplets have no available interfaces. The specification's table distinguishes interfaces available during early boot from the operational memory and input output traffic paths.

This creates a practical dependency test. If firmware must be loaded before the operational memory interface exists, that interface cannot be the only means of establishing the earlier state. The boot path needs an available mechanism at the point where it is used. Some implementation rules allow memory interfaces as alternatives when those interfaces are already available; the condition is part of the rule.

Do the same check for low-power behavior. A control message needed to leave a state cannot depend on a path disabled in that state unless another specified mechanism restores it. Use the particular pair's requirements as well as the summary table; examples of availability are not a substitute for all applicable rules.

Workbook exercise three gives you a proposed boot dependency. Identify what must happen first, mark the unavailable path, and propose the evidence needed to establish a usable alternative. The exercise is about resolving the dependency and its ownership. It does not ask you to invent the protocol entries that F C S A leaves open.
rows: Are the required security, control, and image-load paths available?
Are the high-capacity functional interfaces ready?
Which low-power or dedicated paths remain usable?

slides.title: Three boot models, coordinated progress
slides.transcript: Follow the second-stage boot image, then ask who controls progress. In distributed boot, the manager fetches both images from one nonvolatile memory and loads the subordinate's image into that component. In shared boot, each component fetches its own image from the same memory. Sequence control manages access and controls when images execute. In independent boot, each component loads from separate memory, potentially in parallel. The components still synchronize; separate storage does not remove coordination. Ready to proceed and Error travel from subordinate to manager. Proceed travels back. Depending on the model and step, those signals govern loading, execution, or synchronization. Keep the image path separate from permission to advance. An error reports a loading or verification problem; it is not permission to continue. These examples concern second-stage boot. The signals alone neither authenticate the firmware nor define a complete boot protocol.

figure.alt: Compare image delivery routes separately from Ready to proceed, Proceed, and Error. Signaling coordinates progress; authentication needs its own evidence.
figure.caption: The three loading models change the image route. Sequence control separately coordinates progress.

slides.title: Coordinate control and establish trust
slides.transcript:
The System Control Framework performs low-level system management, including power and thermal management. One primary system controller coordinates secondary system controllers. A controller sets policy within its scope, while system control agents implement policy directly or locally. These roles explain how a distributed system can coordinate actions without making every chiplet an equal policy authority.

Trusted Security Agents provide a different set of functions. They implement hardware-enforced security responsibilities and the security-platform roles used to establish and maintain trust. Both control and security components can execute firmware and participate in boot, but a shared implementation technology does not make their architectural responsibilities identical. A power-state decision is not itself an attestation decision.

Return to the accelerator case. Identify the owner of a requested reset, the agent that acts locally, and the security consequences of changing state. A reset may require coordinated resource management and also invalidate security evidence. Describe those two effects explicitly. If a supplier names one management block, ask which roles it actually implements and which interfaces protect the relevant exchanges.

Spend about seven minutes completing exercise three, including the role map. The worked response shows how to separate the early-boot dependency from the authority questions. That separation gives the security review in the next module a concrete system to assess, instead of a vague assumption that the controller handles everything.

slides.title: Build security around the composed system
slides.transcript: Disaggregation changes the places where identity, state, and responsibility must be established. This module explains F C S A's chiplet-system security model and applies it to two integration risks. The objective is system security comparable to the monolithic case, evaluated in product context. The chapter is a starting point for that analysis, not a certificate that any selected composition is secure.

slides.transcript: Locate the protected assets and boundaries first. Then trace chiplet-local evidence to the system root of trust and examine what changes when debug or firmware state changes. Workbook exercise four records the policy, evidence, response, and residual-risk reasoning for the accelerator case.

slides.title: A package boundary does not establish trust
slides.transcript:
A package can contain chiplets from different suppliers and lifecycle histories. Physical enclosure does not establish identity, acceptable firmware, authorized debug state, or the intended topology. Those properties need evidence and policy. The security analysis begins with the assets, actors, and access paths that matter to the product.

F C S A distinguishes intra-chiplet domains from inter-chiplet domains. A bound inter-chiplet domain is composed through controlled trust relationships; attachable relationships have a different boundary and assumptions. Do not infer the security domain solely from a package outline. The question is which components and paths participate in a protected relationship and how that relationship is established and maintained.

For the accelerator case, identify valuable firmware, keys, system memory, configuration, and the evidence used to decide trust. Then consider who could alter the chiplet or reach debug and test mechanisms during manufacturing, integration, service, or operation. A controlled supply chain can affect the assessment only when product evidence supports the assumption and shows how it is maintained.

The chapter's SoC-equivalent security objective guides analysis across disaggregation. It does not supply definitive requirements for every product or replace a relevant assurance framework. Use the model to ask what security property could be lost at a newly exposed boundary, then identify the mechanisms and evidence needed to preserve it.

slides.title: From local evidence to system trust
slides.transcript: A chiplet can report its identity and security state without deciding whether the whole system should trust the composition. Its chiplet root of trust for attestation, or C rot A, supplies local evidence and retains local security responsibilities. The System Root of Trust appraises that evidence against trusted references, the intended composition, and system policy. It checks freshness and the participating chiplets' roles and topology before deciding whether the Security Platform can form or continue. Optional Secondary Chiplet Roots of Trust can provide additional services. They do not make the system-level composition decision. Now change a participating chiplet's debug state. The earlier evidence describes an earlier state. Revalidation is required, just as after a security-relevant update, reset, or recovery. Keep evidence, policy, and response connected throughout operation. A valid identity alone is not a maintained system trust decision.

slides.title: Turn a threat into a justified mitigation
slides.transcript:
Work from a concrete threat rather than a list of security features. Suppose an unauthorized accelerator is substituted during integration. Identify the threatened asset and adversary, then ask what identity and composition evidence would expose the substitution. Authentication alone is incomplete if any authentic device is accepted: the system must compare the observed chiplet and its role with the authorized composition. The policy also needs a defined response when that comparison fails.

Now consider an accelerator whose debug state permits access inconsistent with operation. Evidence must describe the relevant state, and the system needs an enforced response if the state changes. Merely logging the event does not show that sensitive assets are protected. A restricted bootstrap state, isolation, recovery, or another product-defined action needs validation against the particular threat and operating constraints.

F C S A uses Control, Accept, Suppress, and Transfer as the four treatment categories, abbreviated cast. Choose a treatment with a reason. Explain the initial likelihood and impact, the mitigation mechanism, the remaining risk, and the evidence supporting the conclusion. The chapter's generic ratings are starting points, not measurements of your product. Do not copy a lower residual rating without the evidence and validated response that justify it.

Exercise four uses these two threats to practice a compact review. The full specification catalog contains twenty named threats; the two examples are not a complete product threat model.

slides.title: Trust must survive change
slides.transcript:
A trust decision describes an accepted state; it is not permanent permission detached from that state. Firmware update, reset, warm reset, chiplet fault, debug unlock, and recovery can change the basis of composition assurance. The system root of trust must trigger revalidation when such a change can affect the Security Platform. Chiplet-local enforcement and reporting remain important during runtime.

Freshness matters because a report describing yesterday's accepted state cannot establish the current state after a change. Rollback and revocation status matter because an apparently authentic identity or image may no longer be authorized. Topology and role bindings matter because moving a valid component into a different composition can change its security effect. The review should connect each relevant event to the evidence that becomes stale and to the authority responsible for responding.

Spend about eight minutes on exercise four. Pick one state change for the accelerator, identify the invalidated assumption, and define what the product does until appraisal succeeds. Then state the evidence needed to validate that response. If the product relies on an external verifier that is unavailable early in boot, the policy must preserve a restricted bootstrap state until the necessary appraisal succeeds. Do not solve that dependency by assuming the complete Security Platform already exists; formation must not depend on services available only after formation.

cards.title: Reappraise

cards.title: Respond
cards.body: Maintain a defined restricted or recovery state until policy conditions are met.

slides.title: Security is a maintained system property
slides.transcript: Security depends on an authorized composition and maintained conditions. Local chiplet evidence and a system-level appraisal are distinct responsibilities. The threat catalog helps structure product-specific reasoning, while a mitigation needs evidence for its effect and its response. You have now connected a state change to revalidation and residual risk. The integration review must carry those obligations alongside functionality, boot, and scalability.

slides.title: Evaluate integration readiness and future profiles
slides.transcript: A scoped type claim is a starting point for integration, not the end of the review. This module combines the architectural decisions into an evidence worksheet, examines two system-level constraints, and considers why a market profile may add requirements. The Physical A I workstream presented at the twenty twenty-six O C P Global Summit is our example of proposed extension work, distinct from the published F C S A requirements.

slides.title: The evidence you will request
slides.transcript: Follow one transaction across a property mismatch, then widen the view to system capacity. Build the evidence worksheet from the system boundary through trust and lifecycle behavior. Finally, vary the accelerator case for a robotics deployment. You will identify what the published foundation answers and which timing, safety, and deployment agreements still need definition.

slides.title: Compatible types still need a system check
slides.transcript: Matching chiplet types is only the start of an integration review. Follow a memory transaction between two chiplets whose interconnect properties differ, such as address-field or identifier-field width. The transaction must be adapted as needed before it crosses the chiplet memory traffic interface. The relevant protocol determines the adaptation; changing the drawing's field shape does not authorize dropping information. The differences must not prevent transmission or reception, or the required performance of related system functions. Those requirements need evidence for the actual design. Now widen the view. A snoop filter can serve coherent caches on several chiplets. Adding a requester chiplet changes the combined demand that its capacity must support. A chiplet-local capacity statement is therefore insufficient. Evaluate the participating system together. F C S A places transaction adaptation in Level One and the combined snoop-filter capacity rule in Full compliance.

slides.title: Build the integration evidence worksheet
slides.transcript:
The worksheet joins the decisions from the course without pretending to replace the specification. Start with the system software boundary and intended configuration. Record the specification version, system type, chiplet types, and compliance level. Then link every critical interface to its function, protocol, transport, version compatibility, and state availability. Mark unresolved mappings and additional design or profile requirements explicitly.

Record boot ownership separately from security acceptance. Identify the image source, loading model, synchronization authority, and authentication responsibilities. Include the system-control roles and the policy governing reset and power changes. For trust, request evidence of identity, firmware and lifecycle state, topology and policy bindings, freshness, and the response to a relevant change. These entries need an owner and a verifiable artifact, not a promise that another team will handle them.

Finally, review transaction-property differences and aggregate capacity at the planned scale. Include the assumptions under which the evidence holds. If an artifact covers two chiplets in one configuration, it does not automatically establish a larger or differently configured system. State what would require repeating the review.

This is a course aid for structuring questions. It is not a procurement standard or an exhaustive compliance checklist. Use the linked specification sections to expand each row into the applicable requirements and the product-specific evidence needed to assess them.

Function; mappings; versions; state; image and progression owners
Identity/state evidence; policy bindings; revalidation; response

slides.title: Why Physical AI needs more
slides.transcript:
The Physical A I workstream presentation asks how a shared architecture can serve systems that sense and act in the physical world. The proposal identifies six constraints: deterministic timing, sensor ingress, reliability and safety, security and trust, power and thermal efficiency, and multi-chiplet scalability. These are motivations for architectural work, not newly published F C S A rules.

The presenters map those constraints into ten candidate areas, including closed-loop control, deterministic execution, real-time interconnect, security for physical action, energy management, heterogeneous compute, functional safety, safety management and observability, timestamped sensor data and fusion, and multi-chiplet scalability. The important lesson is how deployment needs become visible architectural obligations across components.

Consider a robotics variation of our accelerator case. Correct computation may still arrive too late for the control loop. Fault detection may still need a bounded reporting, containment, and recovery response across the package. Security evidence may need to preserve the authority to command physical action. Those questions require product-specific requirements and evidence; they cannot be answered by the package's chiplet count or a foundation-level label alone.

The Summit material presents an extension workstream and charter, with proposed future deliverables. It does not certify a product, define A I algorithms, or replace the physical and link layers. Keep that status visible when using its ideas. The foundation-to-design-to-profile model explains where additional requirements can be developed without attributing them prematurely to version one point one point zero.

slides.title: Review a supplier change and choose the next action
slides.transcript:
The supplier now offers a reusable accelerator with a different boot arrangement, and the product team wants more coherent requester chiplets. A second deployment adds a robotics control loop. Treat these as three changes with overlapping evidence needs, rather than a single administrative update to the parts list.

For the boot change, revisit image delivery, interface availability, execution control, and the firmware trust relationship. A shared storage path does not establish authenticity, and a new delivery path may alter who must authenticate which component or asset. For scale, revisit transaction-property adaptation and snoop-filter demand for the full participating configuration. For the robotics deployment, identify additional timing, fault-containment, supervision, and safety requirements that the proposed profile work is intended to address.

Spend about eight minutes on workbook exercise five. Assign an owner and a next action to each changed assumption. Separate a published requirement, an implementation choice needing agreement, and a proposed future-profile question. Then write a release recommendation in two sentences: what the available evidence supports, and what remains unresolved before the intended deployment can be accepted.

A good recommendation can be conditional. It need not assert that the composition passes or fails every possible requirement. It must identify the scope of the evidence and the decisions still needed. This is the practical value of the architecture: different teams can discuss the same obligations, assumptions, and limits before committing to a system.

slides.title: Reuse depends on explicit integration evidence
slides.transcript: Integration readiness is a claim about a particular composition supported by particular evidence. Carry the scope, type and level, interface mappings, boot ownership, trust policy, lifecycle response, and scale assumptions together. Changes can reopen several of those decisions at once. The Physical A I proposal illustrates how deployment needs can motivate additional profile work; its future direction remains distinct from the published foundation. Your worksheet should make that distinction visible to every reviewer.

Trace functional requirements through protocol and transport mappings, compatible versions, and activity states. Compare boot-image loading models and distinguish sequence control, resource management, and security responsibilities.

Connect chiplet-local attestation evidence to system-level composition and policy decisions. Apply product-specific threat analysis and explain why updates, resets, debug changes, and recovery can require revalidation.
